title: Simple machines
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to name four simple machines, explain how they let a small force move a big load, and calculate the mechanical advantage of a lever.

sections.title: What is a simple machine?
sections.text: A simple machine helps you move a load with less force. Four common ones are the lever, the pulley, the ramp and the wheel and axle. People have used them for thousands of years: ramps and levers probably helped workers move huge stones to build the pyramids of ancient Egypt.

sections.title: Levers
sections.text: A lever is a bar that turns on a point called the fulcrum. A see-saw, a bottle opener and a wheelbarrow are all levers. Pushing far from the fulcrum lets a small force lift a big load. Mechanical advantage = effort arm length / load arm length.

sections.title: Pulleys and ramps
sections.text: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it. A single pulley at the top of a well changes the direction of the pull: you pull down to lift the bucket up, and your body weight helps. Using two or more pulleys together can also cut the force you need. A ramp lets you push a heavy load up gently along a long slope, like rolling a drum of water up a plank onto a lorry.

sections.title: Wheel and axle, and the big trade
sections.text: A wheel and axle is a big wheel fixed to a thin rod. Turning the big wheel or handle a long way turns the axle with more force, like the handle on a well winch. Every simple machine makes a trade: you use less force, but you have to move it over a longer distance. No machine gives you free energy.

examples.title: Example 1: Mechanical advantage of a lever
examples.code:
effort_arm = 2.0
load_arm = 0.5
advantage = effort_arm / load_arm
print("Mechanical advantage:", advantage)

examples.title: Example 2: Force needed on a ramp
examples.code:
ramp_length = 5
height = 1
load = 500
effort = load * height / ramp_length
print(effort, "N")

diagram.title: Trading force for distance
steps: Push or pull with a small force
Move that force over a long distance
The load moves a short distance with a big force
diagram.loop_label: Try a longer lever or ramp

check_questions.prompt: On a see-saw, where should a small child sit to lift a bigger child on the other side?
check_questions.explanation: Sitting far from the fulcrum (the middle) gives a longer effort arm, so a small force can lift a bigger load.

misconception.0: Close to the middle gives a short effort arm, so the small child cannot lift much.
misconception.2: On the fulcrum the child's weight cannot turn the see-saw at all.
misconception.3: Distance from the fulcrum matters a lot for a lever.

check_questions.prompt: Why do workers use a long ramp to move a heavy drum onto a lorry instead of lifting it straight up?
options: The ramp makes the drum lighter
They push with less force, but over a longer distance
The ramp makes the lorry lower
check_questions.explanation: A ramp trades force for distance: a smaller push over a longer path raises the same load.

misconception.0: The drum's mass and weight do not change on a ramp.
misconception.1: Gravity still acts. The ramp just spreads the lift over a longer path.
misconception.3: The lorry stays the same height. The ramp changes how you raise the load.

check_questions.prompt: A lever has an effort arm of 3 m and a load arm of 1 m. What is its mechanical advantage?
check_questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm = 3 / 1 = 3.

misconception.1: That adds the lengths. Divide the effort arm by the load arm.
misconception.2: That subtracts the lengths. Divide the effort arm by the load arm.
misconception.3: That divides the wrong way round. Put the effort arm on top.

try_it.title: Try It Yourself
try_it.instructions: Change the effort arm and the load arm. Can you make the mechanical advantage 10.0?
try_it.starter:
effort_arm = 2.0
load_arm = 0.5
advantage = effort_arm / load_arm
print("Mechanical advantage:", advantage)
